newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada proposes anti-crime gang legislation.
newsitem.headline: Canada proposes anti-crime gang legislation.

text.p: Canada introduced legislation on Thursday to give police greater powers to combat criminal motorcycle gangs involved in a bloody turf war that has killed 36 people in Quebec over the past three years.
The bill would make it illegal to participate actively in a criminal organization, but fell short of calls by local politicians and police for measures outlawing mere membership in a gang.

Authorities would have to prove that the accused person was an active participant in a criminal organization while knowing its members were involved in crimes. They would also have to show that the accused committed a crime directed by, in association with or benefitting the organization.

Canadian Justice Minister Allan Rock said at a news conference in the capital of the French-speaking province of Quebec, that a law prohibiting someone from simply belonging to a criminal group could run afoul of Canada's Charter of Rights, which allows freedom of association.
"You can penalize someone for what he does, but not for what he is," Rock said.

The proposed legislation also introduced measures to support police surveillance of gang activity, would give police more powers to seize the proceeds of organized crime activity and create a keep-the-peace bond designed to make it more difficult for gang members to carry out criminal activity.
"We want to put out of business those whose business is organized crime," Rock said.

Since the bitter battle between rivals Hell's Angels and Rock Machine biker gangs and their respective allies erupted in mid-1994, 36 people have died from bombs and shootings in this province of 7.1 million people.
Almost all of the victims were members of biker gangs or affiliated with them, but the public became outraged in 1995 when a car bomb in Montreal killed an 11-year-old boy.
Terrified residents in several Quebec communities have protested the gangs' penchant for using bombs.
At stake in the gang war is the control of the lucrative illegal drug trade and contraband alcohol and cigarettes.
Rock said the proposed law was aimed at fighting gang activity across Canada, not just the biker groups in Quebec.
"Organized crime is a national scourge," he said, adding that the legislation was likely to be adopted in coming weeks.
The Liberal government was widely expected to call a federal election for early June.
